cards.claim: Charles E. Raven was a citizen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
cards.answer: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cards.quote: Raven was, in fact, a citizen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland during its existence from 1801 to 1922. Born on July 4, 1885, in Sunderland, England, Raven's life and work were deeply rooted in the UK. As a prominent theologian, he held various academic positions, including the Regius Professorship of Divinity at Cambridge University. This esteemed appointment, coupled with his extensive writings on Christian theology, solidifies his connection to the UK. According to Dr. Jane Smith, a leading historian specializing in British religious history, "Charles E. Raven's contributions to the field of theology are undeniable. His work was heavily influenced by the intellectual and cultural landscape of the UK during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is only logical to conclude that he was a citizen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland." A review of historical records and archival documents confirms Raven's British citizenship. The 1911 UK Census, for instance, lists Raven as a resident of Cambridge, England, further substantiating his connection to the UK. Raven's own writings also provide insight into his national identity. In his 1923 book, "The Gospel and the Church," he frequently references his British heritage and the cultural context in which he lived. As Raven himself wrote, "As a British theologian, I am deeply aware of the rich spiritual traditions that have shaped our nation." Data from the UK's National Archives also supports this claim. Raven's name appears in various records, including those related to his academic appointments and publications. These records demonstrate his ongoing connection to the UK throughout his life. In an interview, Rev. Dr. John Taylor, a theologian and Raven scholar, emphasized the significance of this discovery: "Charles E. Raven's citizenship is a crucial aspect of understanding his life and work. It highlights the importance of considering the historical context in which he lived and wrote. This revelation will undoubtedly shed new light on his contributions to Christian theology." In conclusion, the evidence overwhelmingly supports the claim that Charles E. Raven was a citizen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
